Cholera Pandemics. From 1817 onward, seven major waves of cholera epidemic swept the globe, killing millions and fundamentally transforming public health and epidemiology. The disease, caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, spreads through contaminated water supplies. It kills by causing rapid secretory diarrhea and severe dehydration.

The first pandemic began in the Ganges Delta and spread across Asia between 1817 and 1824, killing millions. Subsequent waves erupted in 1829, 1852, 1863, 1881, 1899, and 1961 through 1975, propagating globally. The European pandemic of 1831 and 1832 was particularly devastating, killing an estimated 100,000 to 200,000 people across the continent and sparking panic-driven social upheaval and riots.

What made cholera crucial to the history of disease control was John Snow's investigation of the 1854 London outbreak. Snow traced deaths to the Broad Street pump, proving the waterborne transmission route and pioneering epidemiological detective work. Unlike plague, cholera was associated with poverty and poor sanitation. Urban centers with inadequate sewage systems suffered catastrophic mortality.

This pandemic prompted the creation of modern water treatment systems, sewage infrastructure, and international disease reporting. These innovations became the foundations of epidemiology and public health. The seventh pandemic, beginning in 1961 and continuing today, is caused by the El Tor biotype, which is less virulent but more transmissible than earlier strains.
